hook: **Retrieval can't fix bad chunks.** Ingestion and chunking decide 80% of RAG quality — before any embedding exists. This reel is the craft.

scenes.title: Every file format is a **liar** in its own way
scenes.sub: Parsing is where clean-looking documents reveal their true mess
scenes.narration: Before any chunking, you must extract text — and every format hides traps. PDF is a layout format, not a text format: what looks like a paragraph is positioned glyphs; two columns become one scrambled line unless the parser understands reading order. DOCX and PPTX are structured XML — clean, but tables, text boxes and headers need deliberate extraction. HTML brings navigation junk, scripts and boilerplate that pollute embeddings. And scanned documents? No text at all — just pixels, which means OCR: optical character recognition, an entire accuracy pipeline of its own. Choose parsers per format, never one universal extractor.

items.s: Layout ≠ reading order · multi-column scramble · use layout-aware parsers
Pixels → text · handwriting & stamps degrade accuracy · tables need special handling
The hardest case: rows/columns lose meaning in linear text → preserve structure or serialize deliberately

scenes.narration: The parsing horror stories, ranked. PDF multi-column scramble is the classic — text extraction reads left-to-right across the whole page, mashing both columns into nonsense; layout-aware parsers reconstruct the true reading order. Scanned documents need OCR, and OCR accuracy is your ceiling — a five percent character error rate becomes retrieval noise, so quality-check the extraction before you index it. Tables are genuinely hard: a row torn across chunks is unretrievable meaning, so serialize tables with their headers repeated, or chunk them as whole units. Rule of thumb: inspect a hundred random extracted chunks before trusting the pipeline.

scenes.title: How you cut decides **what can be found**
scenes.sub: Four strategies — from naive to structural
scenes.narration: Chunking is cutting documents into retrieval-sized pieces. Fixed-size chunking splits every N characters with a small overlap — simple, but it amputates sentences mid-thought and shatters tables and code blocks. Recursive chunking respects structure: split on paragraphs, then sentences, then words — only as small as needed, keeping boundaries natural. Semantic chunking embeds a sliding window and cuts where meaning shifts — expensive, but chunks align with topics. Structural chunking follows the document's own skeleton — sections, headings, chapters — the chunk boundary IS the author's boundary. Start recursive; go structural when your documents have reliable headings.

scenes.title: Same text, **four fates** — watch where the cuts land
scenes.text: Refunds are issued within 14 days. Digital items are excluded from refunds. Contact support to start a claim. Shipping fees are never refunded.

cards.s: Every N chars + overlap · dead simple · mid-sentence amputations, tables shattered
Paragraphs → sentences → words · natural boundaries · the sensible default
Cut where embeddings say meaning shifts · topic-aligned · costs an embedding pass
Follow headings/sections · author's own boundaries · needs well-structured docs

scenes.narration: Same document, four fates. Fixed-size is what naive RAG does — and it's why naive RAG's answers feel fragmentary: the sentence that answered the question was split across two chunks, and retrieval found neither. Recursive is the industry default — LangChain and LlamaIndex ship it first because it respects natural boundaries at almost zero cost. Semantic is the precision option — pay one embedding pass to find true topic boundaries. Structural is the enterprise option — policy documents, manuals and wikis already have the right boundaries; follow the author's headings. Match strategy to document shape, and remember: mixed corpora can use different strategies per source.

scenes.title: Size is a **precision–recall dial**; overlap stitches it
scenes.sub: And metadata is what makes retrieved chunks usable
scenes.narration: Chunk size trades two failure modes. Small chunks — a hundred, two hundred tokens — retrieve with high precision: the match is exactly on-topic, but they lack surrounding context, so the model sees fragments. Large chunks — five hundred, a thousand tokens — carry rich context but dilute the embedding: the vector averages many topics, and retrieval match weakens. The working sweet spot for prose is roughly two hundred to five hundred tokens. Overlap — repeating fifty to a hundred tokens at each boundary — stitches what cutting broke, so no sentence exists in only one chunk. Then metadata: attach source, section, date, author, access level to every chunk. Filters, citations, ACLs and freshness all ride on it.

items.s: The prose sweet spot · small = precise but context-poor · large = rich but diluted match
Boundaries stitched: no sentence lives in only one chunk · costs some storage duplication
source · section · date · author · ACL — powers filtering, citations, security, freshness

scenes.narration: Three settings that decide retrieval quality before retrieval even runs. The size dial: test against your real questions — build a golden set of fifty questions with known answers, then measure which size retrieves the answer's chunk most often. Overlap: fifty to a hundred tokens is enough to keep sentences whole across boundaries; more is just duplicated storage. Metadata is the underrated hero: a chunk tagged with source, section heading, publish date and access level becomes filterable, citable, permission-aware and freshness-aware. Retrieval without metadata is search; retrieval with metadata is an enterprise system.

scenes.title: Documents change. Your index must **not lie**.
scenes.sub: Incremental updates & deletes — the ops everyone forgets
scenes.narration: The ingestion pipeline runs once in every demo and forever in production. Documents get edited, deprecated, replaced. The naive answer — re-index everything nightly — breaks down at corpus scale: it's slow, expensive, and produces a window where answers mix old and new. The right pattern: track document versions, diff at the document level, and re-embed only what changed. Give every chunk a deterministic ID from document ID plus chunk position — GA-11's upsert lesson — so an updated document replaces its old chunks exactly. Deletes are the silent killer: when a document is withdrawn, its chunks must leave the index immediately, or users retrieve and cite retracted content.

layers.s: Sources polled/webhooked · events: created · updated · deleted
Version check → only changed docs enter the pipeline
Parse → chunk → embed · deterministic IDs → upsert replaces cleanly
Withdrawn docs → cascade chunk deletion · no zombie content

scenes.narration: The incremental pipeline. Watch: sources announce changes — polls, webhooks, event streams. Diff: compare versions; only changed documents pay the embedding cost. Re-process: deterministic IDs make upsert a clean replace — same document, same chunk positions, new vectors. Delete: cascade — a withdrawn document must take every chunk with it, or your system cites content that no longer exists, which in regulated domains is a compliance incident, not a bug. Build this on day one: retro-fitting deletes into a corpus that assumed immutability is miserable.

scenes.title: Chunks are in. Now: will retrieval FIND them?
scenes.next: Reel 31 · Retrieval Quality — top-k, reranking, and rewriting vague questions

recap: Parsing is per-format: PDF reading order, OCR for scans, special handling for tables — inspect extractions before indexing
Chunk strategies: fixed (naive) < recursive (default) < semantic/structural (precision) · sweet spot ~200–500 tokens + 50–100 overlap
Metadata per chunk (source, section, date, ACL) turns search into an enterprise system; deterministic IDs make updates and deletes clean

quiz.q: Why does fixed-size chunking hurt retrieval even when embeddings are excellent?
opts: Mid-sentence splits and shattered tables mean the answering sentence lives in NO retrievable chunk — the evidence is destroyed at cut time
It makes the vector database slower
Overlap is impossible with fixed sizes
quiz.why: Retrieval quality is capped by chunk quality: if the evidence was amputated during ingestion, no search strategy can find it.

quiz.q: What does chunk overlap buy you?
opts: Sentences at boundaries exist in more than one chunk, so cutting doesn't destroy context
quiz.why: A sentence split across a boundary survives whole in the neighboring chunk — overlap is cheap insurance against cut-time information loss.

quiz.q: Why are deletes dangerous in a RAG index?
opts: Withdrawn documents' chunks persist and keep being retrieved/cited — citing retracted content can be a compliance incident
They require retraining the embedding model
quiz.why: Zombie chunks make the system state things the organization has formally retracted — deterministic IDs + cascade deletion prevent it.

code.title: Ingestion pipeline: recursive chunks + metadata + incremental upsert
code.body:
import hashlib
from langchain_text_splitters import RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter

splitter = RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter(
    chunk_size=500,          # tokens ~ size dial: measure on golden Qs
    chunk_overlap=80,        # stitches boundaries
    separators=["\n## ", "\n# ", "\n\n", "\n", ". ", " "],
)

def chunk_id(doc_id: str, pos: int, text: str) -> str:
    # deterministic → re-ingest of same doc REPLACES its chunks
    h = hashlib.sha1(text.encode()).hexdigest()[:10]
    return f"{doc_id}:{pos}:{h}"

def ingest(doc_id: str, text: str, meta: dict):
    seen = set()
    for pos, chunk in enumerate(splitter.split_text(text)):
        cid = chunk_id(doc_id, pos, chunk)
        seen.add(cid)
        vec = embed(chunk)
        store.upsert(id=cid, vector=vec, payload={
            "text": chunk,
            "doc_id": doc_id,
            "source": meta["source"],     # citation
            "section": meta.get("section"),  # structural
            "date": meta["date"],           # freshness filter
            "acl": meta["acl"],             # security filter (GA-17)
        })
    # chunks previously stored for this doc but not in `seen` → delete
    store.delete_where({"doc_id": doc_id}, not_ids=seen)

# Same code path handles create, update, AND delete:
# changed doc → new chunk hashes → old ones purged by the last line.
annot: Separators ordered by structure: headings first → the splitter keeps sections whole when possible
Hash in the ID means an EDITED chunk gets a new ID (new vector) while unchanged chunks are untouched
The delete_where cleanup is the part everyone forgets — this is what keeps the index honest

notes:
# Ingestion & Chunking

## Parsing (per-format traps)
- **PDF**: layout ≠ reading order; multi-column scramble → layout-aware parser.
- **DOCX/PPTX/HTML**: structured but noisy (text boxes, nav junk, boilerplate).
- **Scanned**: OCR only — its accuracy is your ceiling; QC before indexing.
- **Tables**: hardest — torn rows are unretrievable; serialize with headers or chunk whole.

## Chunking strategies
| Strategy | How | When |
|---|---|---|
| Fixed | every N chars + overlap | demos only |
| Recursive | paragraphs → sentences → words | **default** |
| Semantic | cut where embedding distance peaks | precision, costs a pass |
| Structural | follow headings/sections | well-structured docs |

## Size & overlap
- ~200–500 tokens prose sweet spot; validate with golden questions.
- Overlap 50–100 tokens: no sentence lives in only one chunk.

## Metadata per chunk
source · section · date · author · ACL → filtering, citations, security, freshness.

## Changing documents
- Deterministic IDs (doc:pos:hash) → upsert = clean replace.
- Diff at doc level; re-embed only changed docs.
- Deletes: cascade chunk removal — no zombie content.
